UNH.rationale: UNH presents an extremely unattractive risk/reward at current levels. The franchise is genuinely durable — largest US health insurer, vertical integration via Optum, structural demographic tailwinds — but the valuation has disconnected from the fundamental trajectory. Q1 2026 GAAP EPS grew just +0.7% YoY ($6.90 vs $6.85) on +2% revenue growth, with operating income declining -1.4% YoY. Trailing profitability has collapsed: net margin halved from 5.6% to 2.8% and ROE from 22.8% to 12.3% over the past year, reflecting the severe Q3 2025 trough (operating income $4.32B, roughly half the Q1 level). Yet the PE has more than doubled from 12.7x to 28.8x — near the top of its 365-day range — while the stock has surged +46.4% in one quarter to within 2.5% of its 52-week high. The 3.5% earnings yield now sits below the 10-year Treasury at 4.45%, meaning investors are accepting below-risk-free returns for a business whose margins are contracting. The adjusted EPS beat ($7.23 vs $6.61 consensus) and guidance raise to >$18.25 are real positives, as is the +63.3% YoY OCF growth to $8.91B, but these do not justify a 2.3x PE re-rating on a business delivering near-zero GAAP earnings growth. Material regulatory tail risks — DOJ investigations, Medicare Advantage overbilling scrutiny, PBM reform, algorithmic coverage denial lawsuits — compound the valuation stretch. Berkshire Hathaway's full exit is a notable institutional signal. All three pillars align bearishly: deteriorating trailing fundamentals, extreme valuation vs own history, and no near-term fundamental catalyst to justify the re-rating (the Q1 beat is already priced in; Q2 earnings July 16 is the next event but the stock has already moved 46% in anticipation).
